extracted.intended_audience: instructors of undergraduate mathematics / mathematics educators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing and running undergraduate mathematics courses that foster equitable, accessible, collaborative, and authentic mathematical learning. Covers community-building, access/UDL, task selection, assessment flexibility, and modeling mathematical practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of cooperative peer interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Interacting with peers in a cooperative setting is an effective strategy for improving learning and models productive workplace collaboration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage all students to participate but never force participation; be mindful of prior trauma, social anxieties, and access differences. Recognize that students may vary day-to-day in engagement and avoid using those differences to maintain racist or sexist participation patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community agreements (student-authored)
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish community agreements early (ideally day 1–2) that students help author to make collaboration norms explicit and reduce hidden curriculum disadvantages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: give a collaborative math problem for 15–20 minutes, then facilitate reflective discussion using questions: (1) What went well? (2) What could be improved? (3) What are the implications for our work together as a class? (4) What helps you succeed as a learner? (5) Can we come up with a set of standards or agreements on how we should engage with each other? Alternatives: small-group brainstorming then whole-class discussion (10–20 minutes). Instructor may suggest items but should let students lead. Anti-patterns: threats (e.g., 'NO PHONES', 'NO TALKING', punitive warnings) are not community agreements and create hostile environments that disproportionately target marginalized students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample community agreement elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of concrete agreements to surface norms for respectful, equitable collaboration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample items provided: 'Listen to others and be respectful' (give attention, critique ideas not people); 'Be mindful of dominant voices' (leave room, be aware of identities); 'Recognize people are at different places in growth' (be patient, kind); 'Have multiple access points to math content' (technology, pen/paper, make thinking visible); 'Understand mistakes are part of learning' (encourage critical thinking without belittling); 'Encourage team members to contribute' (use power to bring others in); 'Revoice each other's ideas' (restatement for understanding); 'Take care of your body'; 'People need think time'; 'Create structured ways to share and check in.' Note: use these as examples, adapt to local context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revisiting community agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Regularly revisit and reinforce community agreements rather than setting them once and forgetting them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Display agreements (poster/slide) before group work; follow group work with ~5-minute debriefs asking how standards were followed and what needs work. Keep observational notes (e.g., a clipboard chart with columns (+), (−), and 'Quotes') and when highlighting positives use students' names, but anonymize negatives. Even occasional (2–3 times per semester) revisits show that process matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community fun and embodied engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the classroom enjoyable as a way to build community and persistence in mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow groups to name themselves, include movement and embodied mathematics activities, encourage laughter and enjoyment. Fun is not a distraction but part of serious mathematics learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of access in classroom
rubrics_metrics.description: A positive classroom meets the access needs of all members so everyone can participate fully and with dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Access includes opportunities to acquire the same information, engage in meaningful interactions, and use the same services as nondisabled peers. Access spans physical ergonomics, movement/stretch breaks, food/drink/appropriate bathrooms, comprehensible language/communication, and safety/trust/nonjudgment. Ensuring access is both accessible design (flexible practices) and specific accommodations when design does not suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syllabus: Accommodations and Access Statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Include both a legal Accommodations Statement and a proactive Access Statement in the syllabus (preferably up front).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying solely on boilerplate legal statements that push students to seek formal accommodations and may pit students against instructors. The Accommodations Statement informs legal rights under ADA; the Access Statement communicates instructor commitment to creating access and invites students to share needs without requiring a formal diagnosis. Example language is provided emphasizing flexibility, willingness to work with students, and not requiring disclosure of diagnoses. If stated, it must be enacted in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessible design / Universal Design for Learning (UDL)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design learning environments with multiple means of engagement, representation, and action/expression so access is built into the course.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide multiple representations (equation, table, graph, verbal description) and multimodal participation (verbal argumentation, written inscriptions, drawings, embodied movement, gestures, manipulatives). Offer multiple ways for students to understand and demonstrate tasks rather than narrow formats that require accommodations afterward. UDL emphasizes choice and supports diverse learners; NCTM recommends multiple modalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Movement and physical access practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure class to acknowledge limited attention spans and physical needs; ensure classroom layout and activities support diverse physical access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break class sessions, allow students to move (moving desks, short wake-up breaks ~30s), ensure wheelchair navigation and bathroom access, avoid seating arrangements that trap students, allow fidgeting without stigma, and be mindful of proximity for groupwork. Know students' access needs (even privately) to arrange space more effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexible assessments and multiple demonstration modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer flexible assessments that allow students voice and choice in how they demonstrate understanding rather than relying solely on high-stakes timed exams and homework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use open-ended tasks and alternatives aligned to learning goals; involve students in suggesting alternative ways to display competence. Flexible assessments reduce barriers and better reflect authentic mathematical practice (peer review, revision, reflection). See further concrete suggestions in Chapter 6 (referenced).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accommodations policy beyond formal diagnosis
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide reasonable accommodations to students who request them regardless of formal diagnosis or disability center approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that obtaining diagnoses is privileged and inaccessible for some; accept accommodations for illness, mental health, caregiving, religious practices, etc. Talk to students about needs, revisit conversations as needs change, and avoid forcing formal processes that demand energy from students for self-advocacy. Accommodations can include ASL interpretation, alt text/captions, and any supports needed to access learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalizing access talk and check-ins
rubrics_metrics.description: Model and normalize sharing access needs as part of classroom culture (analogous to sharing pronouns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In instructor introductions include pronouns and access needs examples; practice having students share access needs (allow 'my access needs are currently being met' if applicable). Never force disclosure. Use access check-ins during class (e.g., 'Are access needs being met?', 'Do folks have access to this video?', 'What do you need to do your best work?'). Offer anonymous feedback (surveys, exit tickets). Be prepared to change plans in response to feedback and communicate care ('I care about your needs as a student').

rubrics_metrics.name: Features of effective mathematics tasks (group-worthy tasks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select tasks that promote collaboration, engagement, and multiple forms of student thinking—so-called 'group worthy' problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Desired features: open-ended and require real problem solving; allow multiple solution paths or solutions; connect to big disciplinary ideas (conjecture, arguing, proving, modeling, conceptual understanding); provide opportunities to integrate concepts/representations; prompt explanation and justification; allow contribution from diverse skills; low floor and high ceiling; fun/engaging/real-world connections. Recognize tasks won't meet all criteria but meeting more supports productive collaboration. Avoid purely procedural computations that don't foster discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity in task design and cultural/contextual sensitivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider cultural biases and language demands in tasks to avoid privileging students familiar with specific contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take care when using real-world contexts (they can help connection but may favor some students). Design principles: align context across multiple problems, include language goals as well as content goals, and use common language routines/talk moves. Frame tasks openly (not single right answer) to value varied cultural knowledges. Use approaches like Complex Instruction's multiple-ability treatment to describe a variety of skills needed so more students see meaningful ways to contribute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive demand and enactment of tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Attend to cognitive demand: prefer tasks that require connections, justification, and explanation rather than low-level procedural recall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High cognitive demand tasks promote interest and learning; implementation matters—framing can raise or lower demand. Closed framings reduce student-led thinking (examples given: 'Find expressions for all numbers 0–100' vs open 'Which numbers can you express?'). Consider who does the interesting thinking (instructor vs students); avoid teacher-dominated enactments that leave students with trivial computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model authentic mathematical practice (front vs back door mathematics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expose students to the 'messy' back-end of mathematics (exploration, false starts, informal reasoning) rather than only polished front-end results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model struggle, show how mathematicians conjecture, explore, fail, revise, and produce formal proofs later. Create unstructured, open-ended opportunities with feedback so students can develop metacognitive and reflective skills. Emphasize mathematical practices/habits of mind: making conjectures, exploring open-ended problems, proving/argumentation, modeling, and generalization. Portray doing mathematics as authentic, messy, and creative.
